items.body: Label: ACT, 2026 Personnel - Emile Parisien: soprano saxophone; Yaron Herman: piano; Linda May Han Oh: bass; Prabhu Edouard: tabla, percussion, voice. French soprano saxophonist and composer Emile Parisien is an eclectic jazz practitioner with inestimable musical gifts that allow him to explore a whole universe of sound. Parisien brings a glowing selection of tunes composed by himself, pianist and longtime collaborator Yaron Herman, and proficient bassist Linda May Han Oh, alongside two covers. Rounding out the quartet is tabla player and vocalist Prabhu Edouard, who helps establish an organically integrated framework for the leader’s world-fusion aesthetics. This group was formed after a memorable first performance in Paris. Floating opens with Georges Ivanovitch Gurdjieff and Thomas de Hartmann’s “ Asian Songs & Rhythms, No. 40 ”, a peaceful, spiritual tune that, combining Eastern modal traditions with Western classical sensibilities, slowly unfolds with a ternary feel. Parisien employs his intervallic expertise in vibrant phrasing, while Herman evokes distant, serene landscapes. The other cover on the album is Anouar Brahem’s “ Badhra ”—the fantastic opening track of his trio album Thimar—which scintillates with sophistication and enchantment. In the latter, Herman’s clarity of speech and objectivity pair well with the in-and-out lyricism of Parisien, while the duo’s co-written piece, “ Portal ”, keeps the rhythmic momentum going after a dynamic introduction centered on Edouard, who doubles on tabla and voice. Herman’ piano solo on this one is pure delight. On the other hand, Parisien’s “ Bonbon ” is filled with excitement and aligned with Middle Eastern traditions. Herman contributes five compositions of his own: the waltzing ballads “ Olive Branch ” and “ Ruth ”, with the latter acquiring a jazzier, Keith Jarrett-esque vibe before morphing into a more percussive passage over which Parisien’s soprano glides effortlessly; the playful and bluesy “ Nusrat ”; and the stop-and-go flow of “ El Toro ”, a showcase for Oh’s rhythmic adroitness. Sandwiched between the latter two tracks is the bassist’s “ As It Comes And As It Goes ”, a moment of reflection and an opportunity to hear her unaccompanied. According to the bandleader, this is music about peace, poetry, and love, and listeners should be able to feel its emotional appeal as well as the group’s ability to communicate through whatever musical language they choose to mix in. This forward-looking diversity is key, and Parisien’s fusion is not without an airily contemporary touch. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Asian Songs & Rhythms, No 40 ► 04 - Badhra ► 08 - Nusrat

It further claimed that the company was experiencing financial difficulties, had laid off staff, and was no longer able to properly manage the group.

The writer also suggested that UNCHILD could be preparing to disband.

The X post sharing the allegations had amassed more than 1.9 million views. With speculation continuing to circulate online, fans are calling for an official statement from HIGH UP Entertainment addressing UNCHILD’s current status and future activities.

Six years after their last appearance at the festival, BTS returned to the iHeartRadio Music Festival with a four-song set built around movement, transformation, and the group's latest chapter.

Taking over Las Vegas' T-Mobile Arena on 18 September, the group closed the opening night of the iHeartRadio Music Festival, joining a lineup that also featured Cardi B, Goo Goo Dolls, Kenny Chesney, Weezer, and Zara Larsson.

Rather than treating their festival slot as four standalone performances, BTS connected 'SWIM', '2.0', 'MIC Drop', and 'FYA' through one evolving visual world, drawing from the industrial imagery of the '2.0' music video.

The journey began underwater.

For opener 'SWIM', the camera travelled through cracks in a massive concrete wall before revealing all seven members in front of an enormous water tank. Rising water, increasingly violent waves, and flashes of blue and white light gave the stage an immersive, almost claustrophobic quality before the production opened up for '2.0'.

The second track took BTS upwards, placing them inside a seemingly endless warehouse illuminated piece by piece. As the members moved through different levels of the structure, the environment expanded with them — turning their ascent into a literal representation of the set's central idea of progression.

Then came 'MIC Drop'.

Following a blackout, BTS reappeared in silhouette before charging through a tunnel and emerging into a cosmic landscape of stars, nebulae, and galaxies. Where the previous number had moved vertically, 'MIC Drop' pushed the seven-piece forward, carrying the momentum of the performance beyond the confines of its industrial opening.

The night reached its fiery conclusion with 'FYA'. Seven comets streaked across the universe before one crashed into a desert, setting up the final stage. Flames gradually swallowed the landscape as orange beams gave way to stark white lighting during the breakdown, bringing the four-song journey to its explosive finish.

The performance arrived shortly after BTS wrapped the North American leg of their BTS WORLD TOUR 'ARIRANG'. According to BIGHIT MUSIC, the run sold out 31 shows across 12 cities and drew approximately 1.92 million fans, including more than 282,000 attendees across four shows at Los Angeles' SoFi Stadium.

Six years on from their previous iHeartRadio Music Festival appearance, BTS didn't simply return to the festival stage. With four songs woven into one continuous production, the group used their comeback to show where they're headed next.

Ed Sheeran has addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore's removal from his Loop Tour, speaking about the situation and the Israel-Gaza war during his first concert since the rapper was dropped from the tour.

At his Loop Tour concert in Philadelphia on 19 September, Sheeran opened his set at Lincoln Financial Field by acknowledging what he described as "one of the worst weeks" of his life.

"I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," he told the crowd.

Sheeran said that while he had generally avoided becoming a political commentator because he wanted his concerts to focus on "unity, not division," he felt compelled to speak about the humanitarian impact of the conflict.

"What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain," he said. "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic, unjustifiable, and disproportionate."

He added that he was speaking with people "across the spectrum" to determine how he could contribute to helping victims of the conflict.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Ed Sheeran (@teddysphotos)

The remarks followed Macklemore's removal from the remaining U.S. dates of Sheeran's Loop Tour. The rapper had spoken in support of Palestinians during his opening sets at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on 4 and 5 September, where he told the crowd "Free Palestine" and performed his 2024 protest track 'Hind's Hall'.

According to reports, promoter Messina Touring Group subsequently removed Macklemore from the remaining dates after venues indicated that they would not proceed with concerts featuring the rapper. Sheeran previously stressed that the decision had been made by the promoter and venues rather than by him.

During the Philadelphia show, Sheeran also voiced concerns about venues determining what artists could say on stage.

"I am deeply worried about the idea that venues should pre-approve content for performers," he said. "This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world."

The fallout extended to other artists involved in the tour. Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, FINNEAS, and Sheeran's longtime collaborators Beoga withdrew from scheduled appearances, citing Macklemore's removal.

Sheeran brought additional musicians, including violinist Alicia Enstrom, on stage in Philadelphia to perform songs that could not be recreated solely with his loop pedal.

The singer also revealed that he had removed the show's B stage, a smaller platform situated among the audience, because he was uncertain how the Philadelphia crowd would react.

"I didn't know if I would have things thrown at me. I didn't know if people would be angry at me," he said.

Later in the night, Sheeran thanked the approximately 50,000 fans who attended and said he had questioned whether the tour — and even his career as an artist — would continue following the controversy.

Macklemore, meanwhile, said following his removal that he and Sheeran had held "difficult conversations" after the MetLife Stadium performances. While expressing personal respect for Sheeran, he maintained his decision to use the tour stage to voice support for Palestinians.

The rapper has since pledged US$1 million to Palestinian relief organisations.

Sheeran's Philadelphia concert proceeded as scheduled, beginning the next stretch of his U.S. stadium run.

items.body: In musical notation, al niente means “to nothing”: a gradual fading until sound disappears. The title suits this debut by Beatrice Miniaci, Cosimo Fiaschi, Gabriele Pagliano and Luca Venitucci, a quartet whose music is shaped by subtraction. Three collective improvisations sit alongside compositions by Stefan Thut and Pagliano, with gestures pared down to small fluctuations of breath, timbre and silence. The four musicians rarely behave as separate voices. In the accompanying interview, they describe coming to think of the ensemble as “one instrument instead of the sum of four different voices”, an approach that can be heard throughout the record. Flute, soprano saxophone, accordion and double bass converge into shifting composite timbres, occasionally separating long enough for an individual instrumental character to surface before being absorbed again. Stefan Thut’s “Some, 1–4” uses an extremely limited vocabulary of sound and noise to produce a surprisingly fluid landscape. Small differences in duration and articulation create movement within a score that otherwise appears almost static. Pagliano’s “Umbra” is similarly economical, tracing the relationship between a gesture and its “shadow” through minute changes in resonance. Extended techniques belong to the music’s basic vocabulary: pitch gives way to breath, friction and resonance, while instrumental identities become increasingly uncertain. Silence has an active role throughout. Venitucci describes it as a continuous field from which individual sounds acquire their presence, and the album makes that relationship unusually tangible. An attack or breath changes the space around it; a resonance continues to register as it approaches inaudibility. In the closing minutes of the final improvisation, the double bass briefly emerges on its own before the other instruments return and the music slowly thins away, approaching the niente of the title. AL NIENTE – photo by Alessandro Carpentieri To guide us towards silence, we reached out directly to Cosimo Fiaschi, Beatrice Miniaci, Gabriele Pagliano, and Luca Venitucci. Listening to al niente, I often lost track of where one instrument ended and another began. The quartet continually reshapes itself into a single, evolving timbre before individual voices briefly re-emerge. Even in the collective improvisations, there’s very little sense of anyone stepping forward as a soloist. Is that something you consciously cultivate, or does it simply emerge from the way each of you listens and responds to the others? The ensamble: Reducing the material down to its bare bones often implies unison, where one instrument is the continuation of the other. In a way, it felt natural to investigate the unison of four very different instruments, that do not share any (?) musical literature. Probably the idea of soloist ceased to be valid while working primarily with long tones and silences. In both improvisations and repertoire, it seems way more interesting to think of the quartet as one instrument instead of the sum of four different voices. The music we made deals with few musical parameters in which details plays a crucial role: but a sharp attack or a little crescendo, for example, could also be the sings of a more prominent musical action which could be understand as some sort of soloist role. In the last track of the album, at approximately six minutes the double-bass introduces the final with a brief solo. That action, for instance, could be understood as a soloist role, since it’s the only one with articulation, in the sense of density. Stefan Thut describes “Some, 1–4” as a score in which the notated image seems to liquefy when it is brought into sound, only to return repeatedly to its original static form. Listening to the piece, I had the impression that the music was constantly oscillating between movement and stillness, almost as if the score itself were breathing. As performers, how did you approach that balance? Did the notation leave room for individual interpretation, or did it require a very precise collective discipline? The ensamble: First of all, we really have to thank Stefan Thut for his availability and for agreeing to share his work with us. The piece consists of four combinations of the letters x and y, where x is sound and y is noise. We choose this piece for its simplicity within the relation sound / noise, as well as the interest in contingencies, since the individual sound and noise (one for every musician in both categories) are chosen a priori. The piece needs an individual discipline since each performer chooses only one of the four permutation (that is also chosen a priori): sound / sound; sound / noise; noise / sound; noise / noise. The oscillation between movement ad stillness you were referring to is generated through the different durations that each of us gave to each sound / noise. In this sense, it’s amazing how a very limited material (six different musical objects within four performers) can create such movements. Both the flute and the soprano saxophone seem to occupy a particularly unstable position on the album. At various moments they cease to function as melodic instruments and instead become sources of breath, friction, multiphonics and noise, often blurring the distinction between pitched sound and pure timbre. How has your relationship with your instruments changed through working with al niente? Has this ensemble altered the way you think about tone production itself? Beatrice Miniaci and Cosimo Fiaschi: The constellation of al niente (four acoustic instruments without resonances) is the perfect setting to let the subtle characteristics of the flute, bass flute and soprano saxophone emerge through the techniques you mentioned. The air quality is a particular trait d’union between the overall ensemble: the accordion is an aerophone too and the double-bass with the archetto is capable of producing many air sounds. Generally speaking, the overall dryness of the quartet in the discreet dynamics is the ideal setting to dig into the liminal zone between air and pitch for our instruments. Pagliano, in your notes on “Umbra”, you describe the relationship between a sound and its “shadow”, referring to positive and negative sounds almost as if they were photographic images. Listening to the piece, I was struck by the fact that these shadows never feel electronic or artificial; they seem to emerge naturally from the instruments themselves. When composing “Umbra”, were you thinking primarily in terms of acoustics and resonance, or was the idea of the “shadow” also a way of exploring the relationship between action, memory and listening? Gabriele Pagliano: Thank you for you deep listening. The core of this piece can be find in the gesture, or action, as a musical object. Every possible reflection about resonance or acoustic spectrum originates from there: the possibilities that come from the process of transformation, or permutation of a single or composed gesture. Even if the sonic texture has to take a central role in the performer thinking, the compositional approach revolves around this idea more than a spectralist approach in a narrow sense. In this perspective, the fact that we never feel these shadow parts “artificial” it’s a welcomed consequence; I think that the realm of the acoustic instruments it’s were the borders between sound and silence are the closest possible and in this sense the gesture is the device that naturally activates that relationship. Venitucci, with more than three decades of experience in experimental music, you’ve worked in contexts ranging from free improvisation to contemporary composition. What fascinates me about al niente is its refusal to treat quietness as simply the absence of sound. Silence often feels active, almost as if it were another performer shaping the music. Has your understanding of silence changed over the years, and what does this ensemble allow you to explore that other improvising groups perhaps do not? Luca Venitucci: My early approach to sound was shaped by rock and European improvised music of the 1960s and 1970s, and naturally tended towards rather assertive gestures. Later, through Ensemble Zeitkratzer, I came into contact with the Wandelweiser movement and Berlin’s Echtzeitmusik scene, which led me to develop a deeper awareness of silence, not as a mere absence of sound, but as a continuous field from which each sonic event emerges and takes on depth and presence. In al niente, this focus on silence brings the finest qualities of sound into the foreground, revealing the subtle transformations and inflections that arise from each musician’s intentions and from their interaction. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: A veteran of groundbreaking music-video and visual collaborations, Ben Stokes puts his most personal stamp on Dimensional Holophonic Sound (DHS), his singular project blending acid electronics, old-school analog imagery, and experimental video production. Simultaneously, Stokes has built a distinctive career at the intersection of sound, art, technology, and visuals. Inside Ben Stokes’ vinyl obsession Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Benjamin Stokes could exist solely as a collaborator with other artists and his resume would remain an envious one. He has directed music videos for giants like Nine Inch Nails, Public Enemy, Ministry, The Orb and Meat Beat Manifesto, the latter of which he’s also a band member alongside industrial dance music pioneer Jack Dangers, whom Stokes additionally collaborates with in another outfit called Man From Mantis. He has created visuals for DJ Shadow‘s live sets, directed hype video for the Dallas Cowboys, and even helped pull off the feat of M.I.A. and Janelle Monae performing as holograms at each other’s live shows, simultaneously, on opposite coasts of the United States. And this is only a small scratch on his winning lottery ticket of collaborations. Dimensional Holofonic Sound (DHS) however, is singularly Ben Stokes. “I love collaborating with people but I think every artist needs a solo project,” he says. “Something that is their own signature and unique flavor.” I spoke with Stokes—ironically as he took a break from creating visuals for DJ Shadow‘s upcoming Endtroducing 30th Anniversary tour—to talk about his new DHS album, Concept Record, AI art, love of acid music, and any upcoming plans for live shows. “[Concept Record] is kind of like a big love letter to vinyl itself,” says Stokes. “I mean, the concept is, ‘The record is the concept.’ It’s all about vinyl. It’s an art object. I went to art school and I was trained to make objects, so it was very important to me.” That love of records is so grand that he took a risk, spent the extra money on the bells and whistles—including fifteen lock-groove loop tracks—and wrote his love letter on a hand-crafted double-vinyl edition of the album engineered with Anne-Marie Suenram of Suenram Productions in San Pablo, California, the only woman-owned and operated cutting and mastering company of its kind in North America. Ben Stokes and Anne-Marie Suenram engineering the lacquer cut for the vinyl edition of Concept Record. Taken from Stokes’ Instagram page. Locking into the groove :: Cutting the vinyl with its special features was a true labor of love. “It was indeed a major learning experience that challenged me to apply everything I’d learned,” Suenram says via email, “but with Ben‘s encouragement I was able to figure out what I needed to do. Ben‘s record was, and still is, the only record I’ve done with this kind of cut,” she says. “I wanted to try to do all the kind of physical, fun things that you can do only with vinyl,” Stokes continues, “like lock-grooves, beat matching and putting things at 133.33 beats per minute, which if you look at those tracks that are at that tempo, the grooves on the physical record actually kind of line up in an interesting visual way. And um, little side note, the inner disk labels, if you set your phone to 30 frames a second [and record a video] you get some semblance of a little animation there.” Honing in specifically on the logistics of creating a record with so many lock-groove tracks, Stokes brought along a favorite record from his collection called 500 Lock-Grooves By 500 Artists as a template. “Anywhere you drop the needle, it locks. [Suenram] looked at that record under a microscope and she was like, ‘I’m not sure how they did this, and we can’t do it quite this way with my machinery,'” Stokes explains. “The workaround was to create sort of like an entry ramp onto a freeway,” he says, “so there’s a little silence before each lock groove, and then it locks. It circles in on itself. And you really can’t test it, so you don’t really know if it’s going to work until you get your test pressings and at that point, I was like, well, I’m not going back.” Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff :: Lucky for him, as well as for us, it worked very well and serves as another feature of the record’s concept, which is mixing the two records with each other—or with other records—on turntables. Stokes has done DJ sets with the album already, using his 500 Lock-Grooves record alongside Concept Record, and says they worked perfectly together. “Every lock groove on any record will match up with any lock groove on any other record, if you’re playing at the same speed.” He encourages musicians and DJs to post their own mixes to Instagram. “I would love to see what people do,” he says excitedly. All of these nifty features would be mere window dressing without solid DHS music at the core. “I didn’t want it to overshadow that it’s also a new DHS record,” says Stokes. “Part of it came about because I stumbled into a really funny sample, and it’s basically like [a celebrity] interviewing himself, and he’s talking about his album, and he’s like, ‘Oh, it’s just a great album. I mean, it’s what they call a concept record.’ So, that kind of sent me in that trajectory… led me down a rabbit hole. After that initial, like, kind of inspiration, then I just threw in every sample that I have of people talking about records. It’s got some acid house tracks and some minimal electronic-y stuff. I don’t know, signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff.” A good portion of Concept Record is dedicated to the acid music style DHS is known for. From dropping the “Green Acid” and subsequently being treated in the “Hospital Tent,” to the reminder of “I Can Feel It,” blooping along with “Supersonic Holofonic,” then flashing back with “Cut To Black” and “Full Blackout,” the whole middle section plays like one big, aural, acid-trip. “Yeah, there is kind of like a little storyline there,” admits Stokes. When asked what draws him to the style, he replies, “It was seminal. I went to school in Chicago in 1986, and the whole house thing was just teetering into acid. I don’t even think the term acid in 1986 was prevalent. But I was schooled on that stuff through WBMX radio in Chicago where, literally, I mean, the entire city would be listening to the same station. You’d hear it coming out of cars. On your front stoop, you’d hear it, one car going by with the Doppler effect, and you’d hear another one on the same station come in the other direction. I mean, it was just such a magical time. I was so young and that music was just totally new and unlike anything else that I had ever heard. I already loved electronic stuff, but this was just like, wow, these endless mixes of pretty much anonymous stuff WBMX would play for 4 hours on Friday and Saturday night. So that was just a really formative time for me. Definitely a really cool time, I think, for music.”   Redefining The Concept Record :: Now 40 years removed from those halcyon college days, the imagery Stokes has created for Concept Record‘s gatefold cover is decidedly 2026. While the content of many of the pictures may evoke the 1950s and 1960s in style, the artificial intelligence used to create them, as well as the music video for the album’s title track, “Concept Record​,” is apparent. “I actually hate AI,” Stokes says. “If I had found some film about a company that made a shiny silver record and everyone was analyzing it, I’m sure I would have used that.” He underscores that working in the industry he’s in, often being called in by companies as an art director for audio/visual projects, “You gotta keep up with the new tools. I spent a year just learning how to use some of the AI tools.” For Stokes it’s a reflection of this moment in time, yet he still tried to approach it from a familiar standpoint. “In a lot of ways, these images for the cover and for that video were very much like creating stock footage from possibly old educational films or something like that. I just created them in a very different way,” he says. “But it felt kind of familiar territory for me because I was thinking of it like stock footage.” Don’t expect AI creation to be the new norm for Stokes though. “You mentioned the ‘Supersonic [Holofonic]’ video,” he says, which I indeed had. “Well, that’s all found-footage. That’s very DHS.” He continues, “I’m sure that I will use [AI] again for work things, but when it comes to DHS stuff I think I’m going old school for everything going forward. It was an interesting detour and I feel like that’s something that, as an artist, I do often,” he says. “I did that video, I did this album cover, and then I canceled all my subscriptions. I’m going back to my roots. I like going outside with my camera and shooting stuff or doing stop motion animation. And I think that people are kind of probably craving a little bit more rough-around-the-edges analog look, you know?” Stokes stresses as to the musical content, “I did put a very big disclaimer on the inside that no audio was created using AI.”   The Art of the Tease :: With Concept Record being Ben Stokes‘ ode to the vinyl record, it almost begs the question as to what he’s been spinning lately. “I’ve been really getting into 45s,” he says. “I go up to my mom’s cabin in northern Minnesota and there’s like this thrift store called Rick’s Relics in Tower, Minnesota, and they just have this phenomenal collection of records. Just boxes and boxes and piles that, you know, they’re all out of their sleeves. It’s like 25 cents for a 7-inch. And I’ve been picking up all kinds, like The Trashmen, a Minneapolis band from the 60s. They’re, like, garage surf sort of style. I love a lot of that shit.” In continuing to answer the same question, Stokes pivots to Meat Beat Manifesto. “I absolutely love everything Jack [Dangers] does. I think it’s just incredible.” He admits to a little name dropping on his album. “I had to name-call Meat Beat Manifesto by naming a song, “Meat Beat Manifesto Soundcheck.” That was us at a show, doing soundcheck for a show.” Casually in the conversation Stokes drops a bombshell: “There is going to be a Meat Beat Manifesto tour early next year.” Cue the sound of a needle scratching across a record. “We’re booked to do a couple shows in Europe, and then there’s going to be some dates here [in the U.S.]. And, um, more info to come! And at some point, Jack and I are going to do probably a [Man From] Mantis album. Sometime in the, uh, indefinite future,” he teases. Does this mean new Meat Beat material is around the corner? “Yeah, well, Jack‘s always, always got new stuff coming out,” is the response. What of a DHS live tour supporting Concept Record though? “Well, I would love to,” says Stokes. “I’m trying to figure out a stealthy version that I can fit in the trunk of my car and like, you know, do at least a small mini tour. LA, I think, is pretty conceivable. And of course, when we do shows locally here in San Francisco, I get the absolute pleasure of having Jack performing with me as DHS.” You might guess what Stokes offers next: “I’m just going to have to keep you posted on that.” Perhaps Ben Stokes just came up with his next concept: The Art of the Tease. If so, it’s coming along nicely. Concept Record is available on Bandcamp. Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound    The post Chit Chat with Ben Stokes of Dimensional Holofonic Sound first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: From its roots as a music blog to a fiercely independent label built around physical releases, Somewherecold Records has grown from Jason Lamoreaux’s love of experimental music into a deeply personal effort to give artists and their work something lasting to hold onto. There’s (still) a chill in the air… Déka by The Corrupting Sea   When did Somewherecold Records start, and what was your inspiration? Jason Lamoreaux :: The original version of the label was a partnership with another label in Texas. I think we put out 8 or so albums with them. In 2008, the blog shut down for really accidental reasons and I wanted to start it back up again in 2016. Part of the initiative was the fact that I started to record under The Corrupting Sea and wanted to put my own music out because I thought no one else would care (I’m glad I was very wrong). Anyway, I was a shoegaze DJ at the time and ran into The Beremy Jet‘s EPs but they had no physical release. For me, digital only is a travesty for many albums. I’m very much a physical media person because the entire package is the album. I love putting artwork together, getting the right combination of packaging, and offering the world something to actually hold. Perhaps that’s the Gen Xer in me but I can’t get beyond it really. So, once The Beremy Jets was on board, I began reaching out to folks I had interviewed or reviewed or I was a fan of and brought some into the label. As of now, the roster has been whittled down extensively due to money, health issues, and just the world in general seeming to reject art (perhaps out of financial desperation or something other). At the end of the day, I just want to leave something beautiful behind in this world. The structure of the label is very much inspired by Daniel Miller and the early Mute Records approach to artists. He did it right with honor. He can sleep at night while I don’t know how other record label CEOs can (I’m speaking primarily about major labels that rip off their artists). Anyway, That’s the short of it. Who were some of your initial artist relations, and did your location help or hinder progress? Jason Lamoreaux :: I started the label while living in Texas. I hadn’t gotten to the point where I wanted to play live or even had figured out how to do so with what I was putting together. The location however was great because there are so many experimental artists in Dallas and Austin and getting to cut my teeth live in those places was a huge challenge and inspiration. I didn’t get any on the label till later for some reason, but the label was young and others had different outlets. Initial artists included Aidan Baker, Ummagma, Mis+ress, Yellow6, Niev, Zombie Girlfriend, Thee Koukouvaya, Winterwood, and then my projects like The Corrupting Sea, The Warm Jets, and more came later. I think I’ve worked with around 50 artists over the years. What were some challenges of starting the label, and how did you envision it standing apart? Jason Lamoreaux :: I’m not sure how to answer this except the Somewherecold reputation was well received in the music world because we did a lot of work on interviews and reviews between 2000-2008. I initially started the blog up again with interviews from God is an Astronaut and The Album Leaf but the label side of things started to overwhelm and I decided to move in that direction for the time being. The label is curated by me and I guess that’s the thread through the label. Walls of sound, intimate ambience, electronic experimental, cowboy drone, and other genres are, for me, deeply connected and I wanted the label to reflect my love for those things. Further, I’m an artist. I wanted to be an artist available to other artists. It felt like purpose and, in many ways, still does. What is your motivation in keeping the label moving forward into the next decade? Jason Lamoreaux :: This is a constant question in the back of my mind. I would love for it take off and people to actually support it in full. We don’t press very many physical copies but the current landscape makes it almost impossible to sell out it seems. There is a lot of noise out there, too many algorithms, and a ton of cynicism. So, in my mind, I’m taking it year by year. Once it becomes too onerous, I will likely walk away and maybe keep me and a few collective artists to keep it going. But, for now, we stay the course. That said, Elasticstage in the UK has made it possible to release so much music on vinyl and CDs over on the European side of things. My first 10 The Corrupting Sea albums are now up for order there as well as all the new releases for the label. It’s a press on demand site and the products are beautiful and sound great. The shipping is very low if you order 3 items (their limite right now per order) at a time. “There is a lot of noise out there, too many algorithms, and a ton of cynicism. So, in my mind, I’m taking it year by year.” ~Jason Lamoureaux How do you deliver the label’s “sound” to listeners and fans (through distribution, campaigns, live shows, word of mouth, etc.)? Jason Lamoreaux :: There are a number of ways. I have a rather large promo email system but that is also an issue since so many get inundated with requests for review, etc (I know you probably get the same). The label does have distribution through The Business in Anacortes, Washington. The place is run by this amazing couple and I wish folks would use them more. Again, getting above the noise as it were. Most of my artists play live but I don’t see that as a deal breaker. A Journey of Giraffes is a studio project and has been so well received. Others are new and I’m not sure if they will play live or not. Again, not a deal breaker. I think people can enjoy music outside of the live world especially considering how terrible support for local artists has become in those live spaces. In terms of word of mouth, well, the silence can be deafening. As a label owner, you often have no idea what fans are thinking, if the label is being well received, or artists being listened to until you bump into someone who tells you differently. You would think that with the mountain of communication options, you would hear things. But you don’t and it can get quite lonely. I do post on social media but I’m beginning to see it as a hindrance rather than a plus. The label is heavily pro-lgbtq+, anti-war, pro-immigrants, and more. The people who run these sites have proven to be otherwise and it’s becoming more and more difficult to justify any presence on Social Media. At this moment, plans are being sorted to go to a singular website with Bandcamp attached and nothing more. Lastly, I have uploaded to streaming, which, financially, is a joke. Does it capture people’s attention? I have no idea. You have to have so many streams even to make a penny. I’m behind on those uploads but the label is in a moment of organization and I’ll be uploading past albums that I’ve missed due to daily life. For me, streaming is not a priority. For the same reasons I dislike social media, I dislike streaming companies even more. Spotify, for me, is now a no go. I refuse to place my own music up there but my other artists are welcome to on their own. I don’t control their music. The Déka box set is encased in a purple velvet box set. It contains the first 10 albums remastered by Jason T. Lamoreaux. All come in artwork matching the box. Also, each album except for Ontology has a brand new track attached as a hidden track. Visit Somewherecold Records: Bandcamp | Somewherecold.net Déka by The Corrupting Sea The post Five questions with Somewherecold Records first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Rather than treating glitch as surface decoration, Signal_Black builds an entire skeletal language around it. What emerges is a unified, tightly constructed collection of focused (yet splintered) electronics—one that pushes exploratory sound forward through distortion, fragmentation, and a distinctly futuristic sense of movement. A distinctly futuristic sense of movement Revealed several months ago in April 2026, this sleek eight-piece suite (titled Disruptive Event) still carries a sense of propulsion and precise direction. From its opening moments, Signal_Black (aka Marcin) establishes a dense exchange between analog glitch and Autechre-influenced sound-design, immediately evident on “Higher Ground.” From there, the project descends deep below terra firma, evolving through scraped emotive melodic fragments and moving further into ambient-industrial IDM abstraction. A fixation on roughened rhythms and microscopic melodic fibers gives “Internal Merge” its distinctive tension, folding broken structures into looping forms that gradually become cohesive without losing their instability. “Long Now” shifts toward wobbling bass pressure, while “TON” sinks into darker ambient territory, and what becomes more evident is that each track extends the artist’s interest in malfunction, texture, and controlled disorientation. As the final pieces move through old-school Arovane-like finesse, especially on “Text of The Present,” “Chronic” delivers a more microscopic form of sonic deformation. Its fractured detail reflects the album’s central idea: a disruptive event capable of interrupting established operations, routines, or systems. Rather than treating glitch as surface decoration, Signal_Black builds an entire skeletal language around it. What emerges is a unified, tightly constructed collection of focused (yet splintered) electronics—one that pushes exploratory sound forward through distortion, fragmentation, and a distinctly futuristic sense of movement. While Disruptive Event channels our favored old-school IDM mechanics associated with Richard Devine, Gescom, Funckarma, Alva Noto, SND, and Funkstörung, Signal_Black takes that lineage somewhere altogether stranger—refining tone, deepening texture, and redirecting momentum into a galaxy of its own. items.body: That exchange between past and present is central to Axial Opposition. Classic Multiplex structures remain recognizable, yet the melodic synthesis gives them renewed dimension, allowing vintage electronic language to exist alongside contemporary detail. A duo creating electronics with melody as its backbone [PCLLP 037] Axial Opposition by Multiplex   Multiplex are brothers Christian and Roland Dormon, their focused frenzy of pulsating electronics sees no barriers, but always anchored by a deep melodic instinct. Emerging from IDM’s early days more than two decades ago—recall their releases with Toytronic, Senton, Piehead, and U-Cover)— they now find a home with Belarus-based People Can Listen following recent releases Colour Kinetica (Bricolage) and Human, I Love You (w/ Remixes) (Clean Error). Their historical relevance remains an important factoid for anyone new to sandblasted, ever-veering strains of broken beats, IDM, and melodic electro, yet beneath those fractured forms is where Multiplex have always been most distinctive: tuneful synthesis, layered with ambient propulsion and shaped into electronic structures that feel both precise and uniquely alive. Axial Opposition opens with punishing electro, eerily transcendental in its summation of the 42-second opener “Reality (Interlude),” before settling into their bread-and-butter language of pristine melodies, glowing synth lines, and carefully interlocked sound design textures. Synthesizers are not simply used as rhythmic machinery here; they carry the emotional weight, allowing melodies to drift, repeat, fracture, and return with a nostalgic clarity. That sensibility comes to life across favorites such as “In Your Dreams,” “Pulsar Energy,” “Verhn,” “Aditya,” and “Neeta_x,” before dissolving into the closing atmospheric layers of “Implode (outro).” “What makes the collection compelling is how naturally those eras communicate: older synth ideas are not merely revived, but repolished, expanded, and brought into the present without losing their original character.” ~Pietro Da Sacco With 24 years now behind Pinghaus Frequencies (Toytronic), alongside earlier productions dating to 1999, Multiplex have long signalled a duo creating electronics with melody as its backbone. Axial Opposition gathers new and vintage material after more than 15 years of silence, sending music back and forth between studios, adding elements along the way and shaping everything into a final mix. What makes the collection compelling is how naturally those eras communicate: older synth ideas are not merely revived, but repolished, expanded, and brought into the present without losing their original character. That exchange between past and present is central to Axial Opposition. Classic Multiplex structures remain recognizable, yet the melodic synthesis gives them renewed dimension, allowing vintage electronic language to exist alongside contemporary detail. There is nostalgia here, but it never feels archival; sounds that might have belonged to another era are given fresh circuitry, fresh atmosphere, and a new context. After such a long silence, Multiplex return not by abandoning what made their sound distinctive, but by reconnecting with it and pushing it forward. A multiverse of melodic electronics, where old synthesis is made new again, and one that only Multiplex can navigate so well. Axial Opposition is available on People Can Listen. items.body: What makes Headphone Beats 2025-2026 so exciting is that it never settles into its own language. Every time you think you’ve identified the rules, it quietly moves the goalposts. Genres are treated less as destinations than as raw materials: broken apart, stretched, folded, obscured and rebuilt into strange new functional objects. Moments of tenderness appear inside the delicate violence Headphone Beats 2025-2026 by Winter Back   South Korea’s Wona returns in a different spacesuit with Headphone Beats 2025-2026 by Winter Back, an album that feels less like a collection of tracks than a future archetype: a visceral, crystal-clear demonstration of what electronic sound work can become when technique, instinct and design aesthetics are allowed to mutate together. I’d hazard a guess it was made through a pair of headphones over the course of a year, because there’s something intensely close-up about it—and the title proposed, eh? On the surface, you might identify glitch aesthetics, but that’s only the doorway. Beneath it are drill and trap rhythms, tensile funk, lo-fi breakbeat trippery, obfuscation, drops, crescendos, proto-brass, rolling bass and complex and simple synthesis that seems perpetually on the verge of becoming something else. I’m genuinely thrilled this landed on my figurative desk. It’s remorselessly stunning. “Matmat” has my heart: thunderous, rolling beats tumble around each other in waterfalls of hugeness and electrification while the low end holds you prisoner. “AGN” stinks—in the very best sense. Its half-time stutter is a screwface anthem of dropping beat and bass pulse, scratch-and-tear music so filthy you can almost smell it. Backward melodies emerge from the darkness to lighten the load, moments of tenderness appearing inside the delicate violence. “There is beauty in the abrasion and an almost ridiculous confidence in allowing sounds to seem to remain unresolved.” ~Will Wonks And this is the crucial distinction: this isn’t impenetrable sound design made to impress other sound designers. It’s a highly informed, deeply nuanced deviance in sound, rhythm and strata. Our title track “Winter Back” demonstrates an enviable approach to drum programming before its apparent mid-point collapse detonates into a spanking groove of epic proportions—the holy grail of contemporary electronic funk. “TLD” may contain the most outrageous break on the record, somehow folding rhythm back into itself and emerging as something entirely new: a funky drummer for 3026. Nearly every track appears to reach a point where it dissolves, sheds its skin and reconstitutes somewhere else. These aren’t conventional breakdowns so much as dimensional ruptures. “Bedrop” is the perfect example: atmosphere and tense pads briefly suspend the album in mid-air before the future-klaxon begins its nagging ascent and the whole thing lurches forward again. “Set Jen” brings tribal toms and deranged circus bells into some kind of beautifully unstable agreement. “Dedication” removes the floor entirely, a beatless blast of aural oxygen that makes the subsequent savagery hit harder. “Starb” and “Still Ago” sound like saucepans being thrown down the stairs through a malfunctioning computer, grinding the listener into submission, before “220” closes the circuit with single hi-hits, elastic wubs and a sense of space suddenly expanding beyond the edges of the record. What makes Headphone Beats 2025-2026 so exciting is that it never settles into its own language. Every time you think you’ve identified the rules, it quietly moves the goalposts. Genres are treated less as destinations than as raw materials: broken apart, stretched, folded, obscured and rebuilt into strange new functional objects. There is beauty in the abrasion and an almost ridiculous confidence in allowing sounds to seem to remain unresolved. It feels experimental without announcing itself as experimental. It feels futuristic without resorting to the usual sci-fi vocabulary. Most importantly, it feels alive. It’s a great example of electronic music one would want to spend time inside, not simply consume. The deeper you go, the more its internal architecture reveals itself: tiny rhythmic decisions, concealed transitions, unexpected pockets of funk, bass frequencies that seem to have their own gravitational field. It rewards repeated listening because it keeps changing shape under examination. You don’t exhaust it; you develop a better understanding of how much is actually happening. A genuinely extraordinary piece of work. A 10/10 proposition where nothing is missing and nothing needs adding. Rare. Welcomed. Headphone Beats 2025-2026 is available on SoundSupply_Service. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Frank Zappa's "pastiche" technique had taken on a new immediacy and a breakneck pace starting with Over-Nite Sensation, when Ian Underwood (saxophones and flute) joined Sal Marquez (trumpet) and George Duke (keyboards) and, notably, this marked the first time Jean-Luc Ponty was a member of his regular band (which included musicians from the Mothers of Invention alongside the Big-Band lineup that began with Waka/Jawaka). With the follow-up album, Apostrophe ('), the music went a step further compositionally, reformulating genres through Zappa's unique stamp combined with the contributions of the virtuoso group he had surrounded himself with.In "Don't Eat the Yellow Snow," he sang rapidly and the band played at a fast pace, except when they shifted the rhythm for comedic effect. This embodied the Dadaist approach that defined his music and his deconstruction of familiar forms, an approach that could lead to paradoxes, such as in "Nanook Rubs It," where he tackled jazz by singing in the style of Tom Waits's spoken-word delivery, ironically, after Waits himself had served as his opening act in the early 70s and struggled to win over the audience. There was psychedelia interwoven with soul, yet nothing quite like what we knew; the backing vocals contributed significantly to the band's sound, a sound truly unfathomable within the Zappa universe.Atonal music, specifically the contemporary classical style of Schoenberg and Var�se (the very same artist to whom Chicago dedicated their track "A Hit by Var�se") could be seen distilled within "St. Alfonzo's Pancake Breakfast." This represented a challenging exercise in synthesizing that entire musical world, an approach he would explore in greater depth years later on one of his masterpieces, One Size Fits All."Father O'Blivion" is a jazz-rock track that shifts into cosmic and progressive territory with effortless ease, a mere turn of a few notes, always possessing that knack for making highly complex music sound deceptively simple. "Cosmik Debris" was a blend of blues and soul, punctuated and interwoven by the invisible, precise stitches of Ruth Underwood's percussion. Zappa adopted a highly suggestive Barry White-esque persona, yet his guitar playing was raw, wild, and distorted; one could never predict where a solo or a riff might lead. He was truly many figures rolled into one: singer, guitarist, composer, and, of course, orchestra conductor."Excentrifugal Forz" speaks for itself right from the title, highlighting the force that emanated from his music during that era, a time when even rock was an indivisible whole. The same can be said for the track "Apostrophe", featuring Jack Bruce on bass, which sounds dense, powerful, and heavy; it emerged from an unexpected jam session and was captured that way forever. The bass and guitar tones of Zappa and Bruce meshed perfectly, creating a contrast that thrived within the stereo mix. It is a tour-de-force, especially considering how the wild playing styles of McLaughlin and Zappa represent such vastly different extremes."Uncle Remus" provided a fantastic counterpoint at this stage of the �lbum, a sort of veiled tribute to Dr. John, featuring New Orleans-style gospel and rhythm & blues courtesy of George Duke. Stink-Foot had a distinctive way of recording the instruments, incorporating echoes, shifts in mood and atmosphere, and killer guitar solos that, much like the electric keyboard, would break into that jazzy-blues vibe.Apostrophe (') is the crucial link that, following Over-Nite Sensation, would give rise to One Size Fits All; it stands out by showcasing Zappa's signature style, transforming what was essentially a deconstructed transitional period into a distinct era in its own right.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — Funny how a riff can sound modern, but I guess that's the way it works. Music moves in waves. This album feels very grabby, fresh and now. It's intricately constructed and great-sounding, ready to put any serious home stereo to the test.Where to start? The singing, where this band excels... and that groove! The drums are as much about rhythm as they are about texture. There's plenty of satisfying, head-bang-able metal riffing, paired tightly with great bass work. I'm reminded at times of classic Smashing Pumpkins, so there must be some grunge influence in there as well.The multilayered male/female vocals is a very alluring part of the PRR sound. Their voices don't just blend; they're sculpted together, fused and purposely locked in?creating more of a Beach Boys vibe than casually tagged-on harmonies.There are some definite Pink Floyd-inspired moments here too, particularly in the 12 minute title track 'Terrifying Angels". Then again, maybe I've got it backwards, the PRR take on it could inspire Pink Floyd. Time will tell, but on first listen, I felt I was listening to a masterpiece of modern progressive rock unfold before my ears. It clears out all the cobwebs of stereotypical prog epics and treads boldly into new cinematic textures and possibilities."Terrifying Angels" is a pretty jarring topic to tackle, so it's probably not going to be the "light" entry in the PRR catalogue. And while there's plenty of complexity and detail here, there's also lots of breathing room. But don't get too comfortable in those quieter passages, there's usually some musical surprise waiting around the next corner.Often the song structure seems indecipherable, dragging you at times through room after room of emotional spaces. I love how the familiar can suddenly become strange and new. The lyrics feel important simply because of the way the vocalists are emoting themAnd a shout-out to "Below Radiance," which really shows off Bruce Soord's skills as a mixer, managing all those incredible, epic synth textures without letting the whole thing turn into sonic soup.The last track, "Hold Your Wrath," is 15 minutes long but is a different kind of beast, not an attempt at the epic in a grand way, but a more understated, meditative journey. It features delicate, beautiful, intimate guitar parts, some wonderfully creative drum work, and I love that electronic bass. It feels like another experimental track for the band, though really, the whole album feels adventurous. And despite all of this, you can still bounce to this band.Prog dog score is 4.5 out of 5 dog bones, or 4 out of 5 for the progarchives system.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — This is actually a divisive album among devoted Yes fans, mainly because of the absence of key founding member and vocalist Jon Anderson. Gone was his distinct and immediately recognizable high tenor voice, along with the more fanciful and fantasy-like lyrics that had become part of the Yes sound. For others, it may be the departure of keyboardist Rick Wakeman that makes Drama difficult to embrace. Filling his shoes was Geoff Downes, whose keyboard approach was quite different from Wakeman's. Although Downes had considerable classical training, his work on Drama placed greater emphasis on texture, tone and the emerging possibilities of synthesizers and electronic technology, bringing some of the new-wave sensibilities of the Buggles into Yes.I recall that sometime around 1980, or perhaps early 1981, my brother and I had each picked up another Yes album. I got Tormato; he got Drama. Neither of us, as very new Yes fans at the time, realized that Jon Anderson wasn't on Drama. Instead, Trevor Horn, known for his work with the Buggles, had stepped into Anderson's shoes.My brother asked if I wanted to trade. I don't remember whether I agreed or not'I liked both albums equally. If I had based the trade strictly on the album artwork, though, Drama would have won hands down. It's one of Roger Dean's great Yes covers.One of the great tracks on this important album is the opening epic 'Machine Messiah.' For anyone who had become a fan of Steve Howe's guitar work and direction on Tormato, this must have been something of a shock. As the track begins Howe goes all-in on the heavy, riff-driven guitar sound here, venturing into territory that sounds like an early precursor to prog-metal. Not that he hadn't demonstrated an aggressive side before, with tracks such as 'The Gates of Delirium,' 'Close to the Edge,' 'Heart of the Sunrise,' and 'Perpetual Change.' But this was different'a heavier, more metallic approach that, in retrospect, foreshadowed the emergence of that off-shoot of prog-rock.The track changes its palette several times, at one point featuring tentative acoustic guitar and an epic, almost devotional or cultish atmosphere as technology is worshipped and revered. It feels surprisingly prescient today. Another major section is full of hope, though, as Horn reaches for notes his vocal cords could barely have been expected to reach: 'Maybe we'll change / Offered the chance / To finally unlearn our lessons and alter our stance.' 'Man in a White Car' is a little ditty that I wish they had developed into a full-grown song. Instead, it serves nicely as a palette cleanser after the frighteningly epic 'Machine Messiah,' which sounds like it could easily have drawn lightning bolts down from the sky.'Does It Really Happen' features one of Chris Squire's all-time hookiest bass lines. Alan White's sheer power and focus as a drummer is especially potent throughout this album, on this track as on any on Drama. The drums and bass feed off each other with near-ferocity, while the vocals are equally aggressive. Squire's distinctive voice shines through on this one, while Horn's singing is also well showcased. Together, they form something of a power duo.The new-wave vibes are prominent in the opening melodic instrumental section, but there are hints of Yes' Going for the One too, thanks to Steve Howe's distorted pedal steel, with his steel bar swooping between the chords.'Into the Lens' is the oft-overshadowed track on this album, despite showcasing the band's hyper-creativity. Horn provides some more emotional and introspective vocals, with lyrics that seem to explore detachment and observation. Once again, Downes' synths transport Yes firmly into new-wave territory, while the song still holds onto its proggy identity through its numerous passages and sections. There's even a wonderfully eclectic mix of sounds, including sitar and vocoder. Howe also leans into his 'talking guitar' sound, using a wah-wah pedal to make the instrument seem to speak.'Run Through the Light' is a rare and daring track for Yes, featuring Trevor Horn on fretless bass while Squire instead plays some affected piano chords around the track. Horn's vocals add a completely new sound for Yes, with a staccato, almost stuttering effect. It seems likely Squire was coaching Horn through the track, and there's a story that by having Horn play bass, the song was more likely to make the final album cut'something Squire seemed quite determined to ensure.'Tempus Fugit' is a muscular song. Chris Squire provides the fast, heavy bass riffs that hold the whole thing together like the bones of a roller coaster. There's also some early use of the Fairlight CMI in the 'yes, yes, yes, yes' synthetic vocal samples at the end. It's an amusing little break in the fourth wall, with Yes seemingly making a self-conscious reference to itself. I can attest to how effective it was: my first conscious exposure to Yes was hearing this song on the radio, and that repeated 'yes, yes, yes, yes' stuck in my head. After running downstairs to tell my brother about this new band I had discovered, I would soon be buying my first Yes records. Ironically, Drama was one of the last Yes albums my brother and I actually bought in around 1980. This is not Yes's best record, but it is essential nonetheless, chock full of exciting music, and everyone in the band sounds fresh and revitalized. I give it a 4.75 out of 5 dog bones. (5 for prog archives round-ed off score)

Similarly to theirdebut album 'Cognitive', but with a greater sense of identity, this 2014 release offers a crisp andcontemporary atmospheric progressive metal sound that features a fine balance between technicallyacute guitar riffs and soothing instrumental liquidity that projects itself in the form ofsyncopated rhythms and dense grooves. There is a bit of experimentation going on as well,particularly in the rhythm section, as drummer Martin Lopez lays down some diverse and delightfulgrooves, perhaps channeling his inner Danny Carey. The vocals represent another interesting part ofthis record, as the delivery of Joel Ekel�f is warm and emotive, definitely befitting the etherealstyle of rock that prevails on 'Tellurian'. There is a certain aspect of the album that is touchingand melancholic, while the record itself is consistent and well-structured, with strong entries like'Tabula Rasa', 'Pluton' and 'Void' beautifully depicting Soen's stylistic leanings. At the sametime, some tracks feel drawn out and monotonous, with a lightweight, atmospheric tone that ismaintained for the entire duration of the songs, as heard on 'The Words' or 'The Other's Fall'. Thiscompletely takes away their compositional edge, and it also diminishes the appeal of the strongertracks. Therefore, 'Tellurian' is hardly a groundbreaking prog metal masterpiece; it is more of adriven and consistent collection of songs, which salvages the weaker moments, and presents Soen as agroup searching for a recognizable sound.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — One could understand and appreciate this Muse album only by knowing that the band had attempted tocreate something completely out of the ordinary even by their own standards. An album that has Queenand Skrillex as major influences is meant to be compositionally intense and stylistically chaotic,which is precisely what 'The 2nd Law' is - a collection of epic, theatrical, and electronic-riddenpop rock anthems that broadly explore the concepts of authoritarianism, power-control dynamics aswell as conspiracy and fiction. A fascinating mixture of disparate styles is at stake here, as theband offers an entertaining collection informed by past releases like 'The Resistance', but leaningmore into the artsy electronic side of their music. However, with its thirteen tracks, 'The 2nd Law'is hardly the most consistent release from the British trio. The futuristic production stylehighlights the strong melodies on tracks like 'Animals' and 'Save Me', but it also renders some ofthe mellower songs utterly dull.The stark contrasts between the funky dance pop elements, the hammering rock riffs, the energeticdubstep beats, and the operatic vocal experiments, however, make 'The 2nd Law' somewhat of aschizophrenic listen. This is effective and engaging for a while, especially when the listener ispresented with excellent songs like the Bond movie theme opener 'Supremacy', the electro-poppysingle 'Madness', or the funk rock number 'Panic Station' in the very beginning of the record, butthe effect soon washes away as certain songs begin to resemble Radiohead or Queen way too blatantly.The two Chris Wolstenholme features are quite good, nevertheless, with 'Liquid State' being animportant album highlight, in my opinion, depicting the band's bass player as a strong vocalists andsongwriter. The two closing pieces are quite interesting as well, despite being mostly instrumentaland vastly dubstep-inspired. I still think the use of electronics and digital instruments on thisalbum is one of its stronger features, but the overall mixture of genres and dynamics can easilybecome overwhelming. I would not call 'The 2nd Law' a classic but I definitely feel it is the kindof record only Muse could attempt to produce.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — *Here Comes the Rain* is most likely the final album by Magnum, a British hard rock band formed in 1972, with 25 studio albums to its credit if you count the two albums released in 1997 and 1999 under the name Hard Rain. With about ten tracks per album, that brings the total to around 250 songs, almost all of which were composed by guitarist Tony Clarkin (he only let Russ Ballard help him with a few minor tracks on the 1990 album *Goodnight L.A.*). This simple calculation highlights just how prolific a songwriter Clarkin was?a rarity in this field. I wrote "was" because Tony suddenly passed away in early January 2024, four days before the release of this quasi-posthumous album.Beyond the context of this tragic event, dedicating a few lines to Magnum in a French magazine devoted to progressive music?even in the broadest sense?is debatable. It's true that aside from the first two albums, *Kingdom of Madness* (1978) and *Magnum II* (1979)?to which one might possibly add the less simplistic half of *The Eleventh Hour* (1983) and *On a Storyteller's Night* (1985)? four highly recommended albums in which the British band seemed to put their own spin on the American formula for full-bodied pop-prog that Styx and Boston had devised with the success we all know, the rest of Magnum's discography offered nothing more than yet another high-energy AOR album.Carefully crafted melodies, a rigid structure that very often followed the verse/chorus/verse/bridge/chorus pattern, and tight, driving rhythms?all of this was far from enough for an audience seeking progressive musical brilliance, despite the regular inclusion on each album of one or two more adventurous tracks with slightly more complex structures.Since the arrival of keyboardist Rick Benton in 2018 (replacing Mark Stanway), Magnum had infused its epic stadium rock with more and more symphonic elements, leaning more often toward the sound of an energized Asia, which made each release more interesting. With its rich sound, finely crafted and catchy melodies, and flawless performance, Magnum came closer than ever to a sophisticated and universal form of heavy prog, quite close to the best of Uriah Heep, another intrepid English veteran. The ambitious *The Serpent Rings* (2020) is a good example of this."Here Comes the Rain" is cut from the same cloth. At first glance, the opening track "Run Into the Shadows," with its unstoppable riff and luminous melody, doesn't seem to represent a major musical shift. Yet hidden deep within this binary music lies a sort of irrepressible despair, a discreet melancholy. And these lyrics, chanted in a thunderous voice, describe our violent world with such darkness that it all seeps into the flashy metal on the surface. This feeling is amply confirmed by the next track, the haunting "Here Comes the Rain," with an even more progressive sound. And what can be said about "Some Kind of Treachery," a heart-wrenching waltz blending symphonic strings and romantic piano?Tony Clarkin once again wrote and composed the entire album but allowed Benton to bring more diversity and boldness to the arrangements (a Hammond organ solo on the boogie-prog track "Bleu Tango," a Moog solo on "Borderline," or classical organ arpeggios on "I Wanna Live," harp-synth sound on "Broken City," and a rhythm-and-blues brass section on "The Seventh Darkness"). Keyboards take center stage ("After the Silence," "Broken City"), while the guitars often remain in the background or provide rhythmic accompaniment, sometimes acoustic ("Here Comes the Rain," "Broken City"). This trend, combined with a greater proportion of slow, melancholic tracks with highly evocative titles (the tragic "Broken City," the anxious "Here Comes the Rain"), and more necessarily binary ones ("Some Kind of Treachery"), where singer Bob Catley?a longtime member of the band whose powerful vocals remain undiminished despite his 76 years?also knows how to be more delicate and moving?all of this makes this dark album more endearing than its predecessors.How can one remain unmoved while listening to "I Wanna Live," with its premonitory undertones, sung with rage by Catley and written by the man who would soon leave this life? I wanna live/ I wanna shout (?) / I wanna live my one desire / Come on and take my hand and walk me through the fire. The magnificent "Borderline," which evokes Rainbow, or even Fish, with its electro-tribal intro and its coda featuring delicate classical piano, brings the flawless *Here Comes the Rain* to a regal close?a bitter and pessimistic swan song, yet one devoid of weakness or clumsiness throughout these fifty memorable minutes.Magnum enjoyed little success in France but great success among our German neighbors, where the majority of their releases reached the top 5 on the sales charts. *Here Comes the Rain* even peaked at No. 2 there upon its release. It is well deserved. After a prolific career, spent largely in the service of a band he could be proud of, Tony Clarkin thus bowed out with what will certainly remain one of Magnum's best albums?an important band worth discovering if you haven't already.

But it is rather enoyleI must say.Well get an extended guitar solo of the best vein. THX to some long improvs during some spacey moments (some might say ... noises) as well as some ''Speed King'' moments aswell as another long drum solo.Next comes the combo " Going Down / Highway Star" for over aquarter of an hour! items.body: Düsseldorf and Electronic music have been inextricably linked for decades. The city has produced a distinctive musical legacy in which experimentation, electronics, minimalism, and a fascination with the future have always been central. It is a history that stretches back to the 1970s and 1980s, when electronic music, with Kraftwerk as its pioneering flagship, was not so much regarded as an exercise in nostalgia, but rather as a way of looking towards the future. It was within this tradition that Mängelexemplar emerged in 2011, simply abbreviated as MNGLXMPLR. The Düsseldorf duo, consisting of Lilli B. and Joa Carisma, found their place in the international underground with a distinctive blend of Minimal-Wave and Electro-Pop. Their name — stripped of its vowels to become the almost cryptic MNGLXMPLR — seems perfectly suited to their musical universe: sleek, unconventional, and just a little elusive. Over the years, MNGLXMPLR have established themselves as a familiar name on the scene, performing at numerous festivals and venues both in Germany and abroad. With their new album, “Neue Zukunft,” released this spring on Infacted Recordings, they continue their exploration of Minimal-Wave, delivering an opus that feels darker, harder, and more intense. I spoke with both protagonists about the album, their musical journey, and the future of MNGLXMPLR. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: MNGLXMPLR has now been active for more than ten years. Looking back, what are the first thoughts that come to mind? What have been the defining moments or biggest highlights so far, and how would you say the band has evolved over the years? M:More than ten years… that’s quite a statement. The funny thing is, there was never a ten-year plan. We founded MNGLXMPLR because we wanted to make music. One year became five, five became ten – and suddenly here we are. There have been intense phases, quiet phases, great shows, frustrating moments, and countless ideas that never made it anywhere. That’s part of it. The biggest change is probably that we’ve become much more confident in our own musical language. In the beginning, there was more searching and experimenting. Today, we have a much better sense of what feels right for MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to turn that into a formula. The moment you know exactly what the next track is going to sound like, things become boring. There have been many highlights over the years – releases, concerts, travels and encounters that happened through the music. But the biggest highlight is actually very simple: we’re still here. And we’re still curious. Q: It took several years for “Neue Zukunft” to finally see the light of day. I imagine that period brought about changes – not only in terms of your studio setup, but also in your songwriting and creative process. Could you tell us a little about how you have evolved and how that development shaped the album? M:“Neue Zukunft” took its time. A lot changed at Carismastudios during those years. The studio evolved, new equipment was added, different projects emerged, and we experimented with different ways of working. Some of those experiments eventually became part of the album. There are tracks that existed for years before they found their final form. We kept coming back to them, changing things, removing things, and sometimes simply leaving them alone for a while. Our songwriting has become more intuitive over time. We don’t sit down and say, ‘Today we’re going to write a minimal track’. A song can start with a beat, a sound, a voice, or simply a certain mood. The emotional side has also become more important. We wanted the emotion to already be present in the music, rather than being added later through production. The result has become harder and more direct in some places, but the minimalist foundation has remained. And we have no problem with a few rough edges. For us, perfect doesn’t automatically mean interesting. Q: What can you tell us about “Neue Zukunft”? What is the central idea or concept behind the album, and how do you look back on the composition, recording and production process today? M:“Neue Zukunft” is about change and movement. It’s not a concept album in the classic sense. There isn’t one single story that you have to decode. It’s more like a collection of different moods and sides of MNGLXMPLR. Minimalist structures, darker atmospheres, harder sounds and emotional moments. We wanted to preserve these contrasts. The visual identity also became an important part of the album. For this, we are working with Düsseldorf fashion icon Ela Holscher, fashion designer Michaela Reinhardt-Beron and photographer Thomas Stelzmann. In Düsseldorf, music, fashion, photography and art have always been closely connected. So for us, this connection felt very natural. But we didn’t want to turn it into nostalgia. We have no interest in pretending it’s 1982 again. Düsseldorf has its history. We’re interested in what we can do with it today. This idea is also carried onto the stage. Sound, visuals, fashion and performance should become part of the same atmosphere. Q: The title “Neue Zukunft” immediately catches the eye – particularly at a time shaped by increasing geopolitical tensions, social uncertainty and war. At the same time, we are entering a new artistic era in which algorithms, AI and digital technologies are increasingly influencing how music is created and consumed. What does the title “Neue Zukunft” mean to you, and how does it reflect your view of the world today? M:We deliberately wanted a title that looks ahead. There is already enough dystopian language around us. Of course, we see what is happening in the world. War, political conflicts and uncertainty are part of the present. But “Neue Zukunft” is not about resignation. It’s about movement. The future is coming anyway. AI is obviously part of that future and is already changing the way music is created and consumed. We don’t use AI to create MNGLXMPLR. For us, the human process remains essential: writing, playing, recording, making mistakes and changing things. Electronic music, however, has always been closely connected to technological change. Synthesizers, samplers and computers changed the way musicians work. AI will be another major shift. We don’t think it makes sense to simply accept it blindly or reject it outright. You have to question it. You have to decide what you want to use from it and why. “Neue Zukunft” doesn’t mean that we know what tomorrow will look like. It means that we’re ready to find out. Q: These days, many listeners focus more on playlists and individual singles than on complete albums. I personally still believe that an album represents a comprehensive artistic statement. Do you think the album format remains relevant in an increasingly fragmented and fast-paced musical landscape? M:Absolutely. A single can work on its own. But an album gives it context. You can build an atmosphere, create tension and connect tracks that might work very differently as individual singles. That’s important to us. “Neue Zukunft” was made as an album, and the sequence of the tracks matters. And then there’s the album on vinyl. We like the physical experience. You take the record out of the sleeve, look at the artwork, put it on and listen. Then you turn it over. You can’t really speed that up. And maybe that’s exactly the point. In a world where everything is instantly available, a record forces you to slow down. You can even hold the music in your hands. Artwork, photography, design and music become one shared object. That still has value. Q: MNGLXMPLR is also very much a live band – you have even played in Belgium three times already. How important are live performances to your identity as a band? How do you transfer the atmosphere of your studio recordings to the stage, and what touring plans do you have in connection with “Neue Zukunft”? M:Playing live is extremely important to us. The studio is controlled; the stage isn’t. That’s exactly why we like it. We don’t want to simply reproduce “Neue Zukunft” live exactly as it sounds on the record. The live versions are more direct, more physical and sometimes even harder. But the atmosphere has to remain intact. The audience also changes the performance. You can prepare a set, but you can’t prepare a room. We’ve already played in Belgium three times, and every concert had its own character. That’s one of the reasons we enjoy playing abroad. With “Neue Zukunft”, we want to play a new series of concerts across Europe. Looking towards 2027, we also want to move beyond the classic minimal scene, discover other Electronic scenes and play larger stages. The visual side will also become more important. Not as decoration, but as part of the performance. Sound, light, fashion, photography and movement should belong together. We don’t want people to simply hear “Neue Zukunft”. We want them to experience it. Q: You come from Düsseldorf, a city that will forever be associated with KRAFTWERK. To what extent do you still feel this artistic legacy among Electronic artists from the city today? Has Düsseldorf’s musical heritage directly or indirectly influenced your own work? M:Kraftwerk is unavoidable. If you make Electronic music in Düsseldorf, you grow up with that history. But Düsseldorf is much more than Kraftwerk. DAF, Die Krupps and many other artists developed completely different forms of electronic music. What connects them for us isn’t necessarily a particular sound. It’s an attitude: experimenting, reducing, making music physical, questioning things, and not caring too much whether someone has already invented a genre for it. We can relate to that a lot. But we don’t want to sound like Kraftwerk, or DAF, or Die Krupps. They’ve already done that – and pretty well. So our connection to Düsseldorf’s musical history is more indirect. You grow up surrounded by music, art, fashion, photography and clubs. You absorb that environment without necessarily realizing it. And years later, you realize how much of it has stayed with you. So yes, Düsseldorf has influenced MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to become a heritage band. We respect the past, but musically, we live in the here and now. Look back. Take with you what matters. Keep moving forward.
